title: Expanding Confusion: common misconceptions of cosmological horizons and the superluminal expansion of the universe
version: arXiv:astro-ph/0310808 (ar5iv render); journal locator not compared (commonly cited PASA 21:97, 2004)
section_locator: Abstract; Sec. 1; Sec. 2 Fig. 1 caption ('Our event horizon is our past light cone at the end of time, t=infinity'; '46 Glyr' particle horizon); Sec. 3 (Eqs. 22, 27, 28; 'Our past light cone approaches the cosmological event horizon as t0 -> infinity'; 'galaxies with redshift z ~ 1.8 are currently crossing our event horizon. These are the most distant objects from which we will ever be able to receive information about the present day'); App. B sample entries
relevance: States the convergence of the past light cone to the event horizon (the finite-openness geometric core) as horizon pedagogy; anchors z_eh ~ 1.8 against our computed 1.87.
assumptions: GR, LCDM concordance model (Omega_M=0.3, Omega_L=0.7, H0=70 for Fig. 1).
conclusion: Authors' claim: particle vs event horizon distinction; past light cone converges to event horizon; z ~ 1.8 objects are the most distant sources of present-day information; superluminal recession observable.
proof_status: Pedagogical/derivative; standard integrals; our recomputation with their parameters reproduced their 46-Glyr particle horizon anchor.
limits: Abstract, Secs. 1-3 key passages, Fig. 1 caption, App. B samples via fetch; Sec. 4 (observational supernova tests) and Appendices A, B fully not read; no volume-budget statement located in passages read.

title: The Long-Term Future of Extragalactic Astronomy
version: arXiv:astro-ph/0107568v2 (15 Nov 2001); journal ref from arXiv page: Phys. Rev. D 65 (2002) 047301, doi 10.1103/PhysRevD.65.047301
section_locator: Abstract; Sec. I Introduction ('moving light cone out of which all distant sources will eventually exit'; 'the event horizon asymptotes to a fixed proper distance from us'); Sec. II start (Eq. (1) comoving distance integral)
relevance: Freezing of source images: each high-redshift source remains visible only up to a finite rest-frame age; redshift and luminosity distance grow exponentially. Key support for the 'signals keep arriving' objection.
assumptions: Flat universe, Omega_M=0.3, Omega_L=0.7 adopted for numbers.
conclusion: Authors' claim: a source at z0 ~ 5-10 visible only up to age ~ 4-6 Gyr; images freeze and fade, never seen at the current age of the universe.
proof_status: Standard FLRW light-cone integrals; Secs. II-III not re-audited.
limits: Abstract, Sec. I, start of Sec. II via fetch; quantitative sections not read in full.
